missions.title: When Someone Is Left Behind

ayahs.arabic: أَرَءَيتَ الَّذى يُكَذِّبُ بِالدّينِ
فَذٰلِكَ الَّذى يَدُعُّ اليَتيمَ
وَلا يَحُضُّ عَلىٰ طَعامِ المِسكينِ

options: Ask kindly whether they would like to join your group.
Tell everyone to ask why they are alone.
Ignore them because you already have friends.
missions.anchor: FOCUS AYAHS: 107:1, 107:2, 107:3   |   CORE VALUES: Dignity • Care for orphans • Concern for hunger
missions.aim: Recognize that religious character includes protecting vulnerable people and encouraging help for those in need.
missions.ayahNote: Surah Al-Ma‘un begins with the Basmalah (not counted as one of verses 1–7).
missions.meaning: Surah Al-Ma‘un begins by challenging the person who denies the final accountability and mistreats an orphan, and does not encourage feeding a poor person. These are serious moral failures, not a description of any child’s worth.
missions.tafsir: Surah Al-Ma‘un joins belief in the Day of Recompense with conduct toward vulnerable people. Ibn Kathir explains the harsh treatment of an orphan as overpowering them and denying their rights, while failing to encourage food for the poor exposes indifference to another person’s need. The verses do not suggest that poverty itself is shameful. Nor should a child think that every orphan has the same experience or needs public sympathy. The Qur’an asks us to judge our own conduct: do we protect dignity, notice hardship, and encourage responsible support? Providing for an orphan or a hungry family is an adult and community duty; a child can contribute through respect and safe, supervised kindness. Our classroom story is an application, never a retelling of the circumstances of revelation.
missions.story: At the Amanpur learning centre, a new child arrived late and stood alone by the craft table. Akhlaq wondered why no one was inviting him. Imaan noticed the child looking at the materials but saying nothing. “We should ask if he would like to join,” she whispered. Akhlaq offered a chair and explained the activity. Later, the teacher invited families to contribute discreetly to a food-support basket. Imaan asked Salamah whether the family could help. Their most important lesson was not discovering who needed assistance; it was learning to make people feel welcome and to support others without asking embarrassing questions.
missions.question: A new student is alone and seems unsure where to sit. What should you do?
missions.feedback: A gentle invitation protects dignity. Let a trusted adult handle any welfare need privately.
missions.action: Invite someone who is on their own to join a safe group activity.
missions.reflection: How can we include someone without asking private questions?
missions.vocabulary: Yatīm — orphan; Miskīn — someone in need; Dīn — accountability/recompense
missions.careNote: Never depict orphans as helpless stereotypes or ask children to disclose family circumstances.
missions.review: What Qur’anic principle guides your choice, and how is the modern story different from the original verse context?
missions.next: another thoughtful way to put mercy into practice.

missions.title: The Small Help That Matters

ayahs.arabic: فَوَيلٌ لِلمُصَلّينَ
الَّذينَ هُم عَن صَلاتِهِم ساهونَ
الَّذينَ هُم يُراءونَ
وَيَمنَعونَ الماعونَ

options: Help only if someone is taking a photo.
Help when it is safe, without demanding praise.
Tell them to ask someone else while you watch.
missions.anchor: FOCUS AYAHS: 107:4, 107:5, 107:6, 107:7   |   CORE VALUES: Sincere worship • Helpful habits • Sharing
missions.aim: Understand the surah’s warning against negligent, showy worship and the refusal of ordinary useful help.
missions.meaning: The remaining verses warn against people who neglect the meaning and duty of prayer, perform acts for show, and withhold even small helpful things.
missions.tafsir: The surah warns against those described as heedless concerning their prayers, showing off and withholding al-Ma‘un. The classical explanations of al-Ma‘un include Zakah and ordinary useful items that people may lend, such as containers or tools. The warning is about hypocrisy and hardness of heart; it must not be used to ridicule a young learner who is still practicing Salah or to frighten a child with a learning difficulty. Prayer is worship for Allah, not a public contest. Sincere worship and everyday kindness belong together. A child who helps carry books or safely lends a pencil can see that ordinary service matters, while still learning to care for shared belongings responsibly. The original warning remains serious; our game teaches the positive opposite rather than assigning negative spiritual labels to children.
missions.story: Akhlaq had finished arranging his prayer mat neatly and wanted everyone to see it. Later he watched Mohsin struggle to gather fallen colored pencils. At first he kept walking. Imaan helped pick up the pencils and asked, “Would you like to lend him our spare pouch?” Akhlaq considered what he had learned about sincere worship. “Yes,” he said, “and we should return the pouch afterward.” He helped Mohsin quietly, without requesting praise. At home, he told Salaam he wanted to remember both parts of the lesson: worship Allah sincerely and be helpful to His creation.
missions.question: A classmate drops their pencils after a lesson. What is the best response?
missions.feedback: Small acts of assistance are valuable; sincerity is not measured by a public score.
missions.action: Offer one small, safe act of assistance without announcing it.
missions.reflection: How can I help others even when nobody notices?
missions.vocabulary: Ma‘ūn — helpful provision/small assistance; Riyā’ — showing off
missions.careNote: Do not diagnose children as hypocrites or penalize missed Salah; be sensitive about borrowing and property.
missions.review: What Qur’anic principle guides your choice, and how is the modern story different from the original verse context?
missions.next: another thoughtful way to put mercy into practice.

missions.title: The Difficult Path of Doing Good

ayahs.arabic: فَلَا اقتَحَمَ العَقَبَةَ
وَما أَدرىٰكَ مَا العَقَبَةُ
فَكُّ رَقَبَةٍ
أَو إِطعـٰمٌ فى يَومٍ ذى مَسغَبَةٍ

options: Leave without telling anyone.
Keep the promise with adult guidance, then enjoy the game later.
Tell the recipients they should be grateful you came.
missions.anchor: FOCUS AYAHS: 90:11, 90:12, 90:13, 90:14   |   CORE VALUES: Compassion • Courage • Sharing resources
missions.aim: Recognize that meaningful kindness may require effort and sacrifice.
missions.meaning: Surah Al-Balad describes the difficult upward path and identifies freeing an enslaved person and feeding others during severe hunger as acts of serious righteousness.
missions.tafsir: Surah Al-Balad asks why people do not undertake al-‘Aqabah, the steep path of righteous effort. The verses give concrete examples: freeing a human being from slavery and feeding others during hardship and hunger. Classical Tafsir treats these as substantial acts of mercy and moral responsibility, not merely kind thoughts. We must not erase the historical meaning of emancipation or pretend it is identical to sharing a toy. The modern child-focused application illustrates the broader principle: help can involve choosing the difficult but right option when comfort is tempting. Older learners can be taught about human dignity and freedom in age-appropriate terms. Families and trusted organizations are responsible for food assistance; children may take part through safe, supervised efforts, without entering unsafe situations or giving away necessities.
missions.story: The school prepared a weekend community pantry. Akhlaq wanted to play football immediately, and sorting donated tins looked slow. “The fun game can wait twenty minutes,” Imaan suggested. With their teacher, they checked labels and arranged suitable food into boxes. They were careful not to photograph the families who would receive them. When the work was complete, Akhlaq found that the difficult choice had given him a different kind of happiness. He still played football, but now he understood that good deeds sometimes ask us to give time when we would rather rest.
missions.question: You promised to help sort donated food, but an enjoyable game is starting. What helps?
missions.feedback: Helping can take effort, and kindness preserves the dignity of people receiving support.
missions.action: Spend ten minutes helping an adult with an agreed family or community service task.
missions.reflection: When has doing the right thing taken extra effort?
missions.vocabulary: ‘Aqabah — steep path; Masghabah — severe hunger; Raqabah — a person in bondage
missions.careNote: Explain historical slavery accurately, without trauma imagery. Never pressure children to donate their own food.
missions.review: What Qur’anic principle guides your choice, and how is the modern story different from the original verse context?
missions.next: another thoughtful way to put mercy into practice.

missions.title: Patience and Mercy Belong Together

ayahs.arabic: يَتيمًا ذا مَقرَبَةٍ
أَو مِسكينًا ذا مَترَبَةٍ
ثُمَّ كانَ مِنَ الَّذينَ ءامَنوا وَتَواصَوا بِالصَّبرِ وَتَواصَوا بِالمَرحَمَةِ
أُولـٰئِكَ أَصحـٰبُ المَيمَنَةِ

options: Display names of students who take supplies.
Keep the supplies hidden so nobody can use them.
Make supplies accessible without public labels or embarrassment.
missions.anchor: FOCUS AYAHS: 90:15, 90:16, 90:17, 90:18   |   CORE VALUES: Mercy • Patience • Solidarity
missions.aim: Describe how believers encourage patience and compassion while respecting those facing hardship.
missions.meaning: The passage names a related orphan and a person in extreme poverty, then praises believers who recommend patience and mercy to one another.
missions.tafsir: After describing the difficult path, Surah Al-Balad mentions feeding an orphan with close family ties and a person in great poverty. It then speaks of people of faith who counsel one another to patience and to mercy. Mercy is therefore not only a feeling; it can mean staying near someone during hardship, making assistance possible, or encouraging a community not to forget its vulnerable members. The wording about an orphan of kin highlights real duties toward family, not a limit on helping others. The Qur’an does not teach that poor people are inferior, nor that a child must carry an adult-sized burden. Patience and mercy complement each other: assistance requires perseverance, while patience without compassion can become indifference. We should give respectfully, protect privacy, and seek reliable adult guidance.
missions.story: Amanpur School prepared a welcome shelf with notebooks, water bottles and basic supplies that any child could use discreetly. Mohsina wanted bright signs saying “FOR POOR STUDENTS.” Imaan gently suggested a different name: “Sharing Shelf — Take What You Need, Leave What You Can.” Akhlaq agreed that nobody should feel exposed. They decorated the shelf together, and the teacher promised to keep it available throughout the term. The children learned that mercy means thinking carefully about how help feels to the person receiving it.
missions.question: How should a school arrange supplies for students who may need them?
missions.feedback: Kind help protects another person’s privacy and dignity.
missions.action: Help organize one shared, accessible item or supply for your family or classroom.
missions.reflection: How can patience make kindness last longer?
missions.vocabulary: Marḥamah — compassion; Ṣabr — patience; Maqrabah — close kinship
missions.careNote: Do not disclose recipient names, request photos, or frame poverty as a character flaw.
missions.review: What Qur’anic principle guides your choice, and how is the modern story different from the original verse context?
missions.next: another thoughtful way to put mercy into practice.

missions.title: Speak Gently to Someone in Need

ayahs.arabic: فَأَمَّا اليَتيمَ فَلا تَقهَر
وَأَمَّا السّائِلَ فَلا تَنهَر

options: Answer gently or ask a teacher to help.
Mock them for not remembering.
Tell them that questions are not allowed.
missions.anchor: FOCUS AYAHS: 93:9, 93:10   |   CORE VALUES: Respect • Gentle speech • Human dignity
missions.aim: Practice gentle behavior toward an orphan or a person who asks for help.
missions.meaning: In Surah Ad-Duha, Allah forbids oppressing an orphan and rebuking a person who asks.
missions.tafsir: Surah Ad-Duha is a consolation to Prophet Muhammad ﷺ. Within that address, Allah commands gentle treatment of an orphan and forbids harsh rebuke toward a questioner or person who asks. Classical Tafsir emphasizes protecting the orphan’s rights and responding to requests without humiliation. A child cannot always satisfy a request, and children should never give money to strangers or accept unsafe requests; the verse still teaches that a respectful response is possible. “I’m sorry, I can’t help, but I can ask my teacher” is kinder than scolding someone for needing assistance. In the surah’s original sequence, Allah reminds the Prophet ﷺ of His care and then commands compassionate conduct. Our fictional scene practices that moral lesson while keeping the special Prophetic context clear.
missions.story: At the school library, a younger student asked Akhlaq three times where to find beginner storybooks. Akhlaq was busy searching for a puzzle and almost replied sharply. Imaan reminded him how uncomfortable it can feel to ask for help. Akhlaq turned toward the younger student and said, “They’re on the lower shelf. I can show you.” The student smiled and went to choose a book. Akhlaq noticed that being patient with a repeated question had made the library more welcoming.
missions.question: A younger child asks you the same simple question again. What is kind?
missions.feedback: Gentle speech can be compassionate even when we are busy.
missions.action: Answer one sincere request for help politely, or refer it to a trusted adult.
missions.reflection: How does the tone of our answer affect the person asking?
missions.vocabulary: Yatīm — orphan; Sā’il — asker/person requesting help
missions.careNote: Do not ask children to handle strangers’ demands or unsafe money exchanges.
missions.review: What Qur’anic principle guides your choice, and how is the modern story different from the original verse context?
missions.next: another thoughtful way to put mercy into practice.

missions.title: Goodness Is More Than Appearance

ayahs.arabic: لَيسَ البِرَّ أَن تُوَلّوا وُجوهَكُم قِبَلَ المَشرِقِ وَالمَغرِبِ وَلـٰكِنَّ البِرَّ مَن ءامَنَ بِاللَّهِ وَاليَومِ الءاخِرِ وَالمَلـٰئِكَةِ وَالكِتـٰبِ وَالنَّبِيّـۧنَ وَءاتَى المالَ عَلىٰ حُبِّهِ ذَوِى القُربىٰ وَاليَتـٰمىٰ وَالمَسـٰكينَ وَابنَ السَّبيلِ وَالسّائِلينَ وَفِى الرِّقابِ وَأَقامَ الصَّلوٰةَ وَءاتَى الزَّكوٰةَ وَالموفونَ بِعَهدِهِم إِذا عـٰهَدوا ۖ وَالصّـٰبِرينَ فِى البَأساءِ وَالضَّرّاءِ وَحينَ البَأسِ ۗ أُولـٰئِكَ الَّذينَ صَدَقوا ۖ وَأُولـٰئِكَ هُمُ المُتَّقونَ

options: A beautiful poster is enough even if we never help.
Faith, prayer, generosity, honesty and patience belong together.
Only counting donations shows good character.
missions.anchor: FOCUS AYAHS: 2:177   |   CORE VALUES: Righteousness • Charity • Keeping commitments
missions.aim: See that real righteousness combines belief, worship, generosity and reliable conduct.
missions.meaning: Al-Baqarah 2:177 explains that righteousness is not mere outward direction: it joins belief with giving loved wealth to relatives, orphans and others in need; prayer, Zakah, fidelity to promises and patience.
missions.tafsir: The long verse of al-Birr teaches that genuine righteousness is not restricted to an outward sign, such as facing east or west. It includes sincere faith in Allah and the foundations of belief, giving wealth despite attachment to it to categories of people in need, establishing Salah and Zakah, honoring commitments, and remaining steadfast in hardship. Ibn Kathir notes this is a comprehensive description of righteous qualities. Children should know that a smiling appearance or a decorative charity badge cannot substitute for conduct. The verse also lists specific obligations and social rights that must not be reduced to a generic “be nice” slogan. Younger learners can study a few meaning segments; older learners explore how faith and action fit together. Giving money and Zakah remain adult-governed responsibilities; children can practise safe forms of generosity and promise keeping.
missions.story: Imaan was invited to help arrange a community exhibition about good deeds. Akhlaq wanted a large poster with his name on it. Their teacher asked the class to think of what people would actually benefit from. They planned quiet reading support for younger pupils, a shared supply box, and a schedule so helpers would keep their promises. When the exhibition opened, there were fewer glittering posters than Akhlaq had imagined. But there were more children reading, organizing, and serving one another. “Our actions are the real display,” he said.
missions.question: What best reflects the message of this ayah?
missions.feedback: The verse connects worship, belief, generosity and trustworthy actions.
missions.action: Keep one realistic commitment to help a family member or classmate.
missions.reflection: Which part of good character is easy to show, and which needs quiet effort?
missions.vocabulary: Birr — comprehensive righteousness; Zakāh — obligatory charity; ‘Ahd — commitment
missions.careNote: Do not simplify the verse into a replacement for its specific obligations. Keep faith articles explicit.
missions.review: What Qur’anic principle guides your choice, and how is the modern story different from the original verse context?
missions.next: another thoughtful way to put mercy into practice.

missions.title: Kindness Starts Nearby and Reaches Far

ayahs.arabic: وَاعبُدُوا اللَّهَ وَلا تُشرِكوا بِهِ شَيـًٔا ۖ وَبِالوٰلِدَينِ إِحسـٰنًا وَبِذِى القُربىٰ وَاليَتـٰمىٰ وَالمَسـٰكينِ وَالجارِ ذِى القُربىٰ وَالجارِ الجُنُبِ وَالصّاحِبِ بِالجَنبِ وَابنِ السَّبيلِ وَما مَلَكَت أَيمـٰنُكُم ۗ إِنَّ اللَّهَ لا يُحِبُّ مَن كانَ مُختالًا فَخورًا

options: Ignore them because they are not a teacher.
Listen respectfully and follow the appropriate adult safety plan.
Ask friends to laugh at their advice.
missions.anchor: FOCUS AYAHS: 4:36   |   CORE VALUES: Parents • Neighbors • Respect for others
missions.aim: Recognize the wide circle of relationships to which kindness is due.
missions.meaning: An-Nisa 4:36 commands worship of Allah alone and kind conduct toward parents, relatives, orphans, those in need, neighbors near and far, companions, travelers and others.
missions.tafsir: Surah An-Nisa begins this verse by commanding worship of Allah without partners, then describes good treatment of parents and a wide circle of people: relatives, orphans, people in need, neighbors of different kinds, companions, travelers, and those under one’s authority in its historical setting. The command to avoid arrogance appears at the end. Ibn Kathir and al-Tabari discuss the rights of neighbors and kin and the importance of doing good broadly. The passage does not restrict kindness to people who look, speak, or live like us. The child-focused application is to treat nearby people with respect, from a family member to the school helper and bus attendant. Children must practise kindness with safety boundaries: no entering neighbors’ homes alone, answering strangers’ requests, or sharing contact details without caregiver guidance.
missions.story: Amanpur prepared for a neighborhood clean-up. Akhlaq signed up with his friends and forgot to invite the building caretaker to the planning discussion. Imaan asked whether they knew where cleaning materials were stored. The caretaker had useful advice and knew which areas were unsafe for children. Together, they made a plan that included neighbors from different streets and respected the caretaker’s time. Akhlaq learned that treating people kindly begins with listening and appreciation, not with deciding everything for them.
missions.question: Your community helper gives safety advice for an activity. What should you do?
missions.feedback: Care and respect extend to the many people who support our communities.
missions.action: Thank one person who helps your home, school, or neighborhood.
missions.reflection: Who helps our everyday life but is sometimes forgotten?
missions.vocabulary: Iḥsān — excellent treatment; Jār — neighbor; Mukhtāl — arrogant person
missions.careNote: Preserve the verse’s historical categories without normalizing exploitation; explain safety and consent.
missions.review: What Qur’anic principle guides your choice, and how is the modern story different from the original verse context?
missions.next: another thoughtful way to put mercy into practice.

missions.title: Give Rights, and Do Not Waste

ayahs.arabic: وَءاتِ ذَا القُربىٰ حَقَّهُ وَالمِسكينَ وَابنَ السَّبيلِ وَلا تُبَذِّر تَبذيرًا
إِنَّ المُبَذِّرينَ كانوا إِخوٰنَ الشَّيـٰطينِ ۖ وَكانَ الشَّيطـٰنُ لِرَبِّهِ كَفورًا

options: Throw all supplies away immediately.
Offer them to others publicly without checking safety.
Ask a responsible adult about storing or sharing them appropriately.
missions.anchor: FOCUS AYAHS: 17:26, 17:27   |   CORE VALUES: Responsible giving • Avoiding waste • Kinship rights
missions.aim: Respect the rights of relatives and people in need while using resources wisely.
missions.meaning: Al-Isra 17:26 commands giving relatives their due, as well as assistance for those in need and travelers; 17:27 condemns reckless wastefulness.
missions.tafsir: Surah Al-Isra commands that relatives receive their due and that the poor and traveler be treated with concern, while warning against tabdhir, wasteful squandering. Classical explanation distinguishes responsible spending from throwing away resources without rightful benefit. This is not a command for children to give away what their parents need or to feel guilty for ordinary enjoyment. It teaches care for obligations and balanced use of Allah’s provision. A thoughtful family can share edible food, reusable learning materials and time without waste, while keeping donations appropriate and safe. The reference to kinship and the rights of those in need must remain central, rather than reducing the ayahs to an environmental slogan. Children can begin by asking an adult how the household can use resources sensibly and support others respectfully.
missions.story: After a school picnic, Akhlaq found several sealed bottles and uneaten snacks left on a table. He wanted to throw everything away to finish cleaning quickly. Imaan asked the teacher what could be kept safely and what had to be discarded. The unopened supplies were counted and stored properly, while leftover food that was unsafe was disposed of. At home, Salamah explained that responsible care includes both sharing and protecting health. Akhlaq decided to pack only what he expected to need next time.
missions.question: What should you do with extra unopened and safe supplies after an event?
missions.feedback: Responsible help combines generosity, safety and avoiding unnecessary waste.
missions.action: Prevent one safe, avoidable waste today with an adult’s guidance.
missions.reflection: How can we be generous without being careless?
missions.vocabulary: Tabdhīr — squandering/waste; Isrā’ — night journey (surah name); Ḥaqq — due/right
missions.careNote: No food redistribution without hygiene and adult oversight. No guilt messaging around food insecurity.
missions.review: What Qur’anic principle guides your choice, and how is the modern story different from the original verse context?
missions.next: another thoughtful way to put mercy into practice.

missions.title: A Seed of Generosity

ayahs.arabic: مَثَلُ الَّذينَ يُنفِقونَ أَموٰلَهُم فى سَبيلِ اللَّهِ كَمَثَلِ حَبَّةٍ أَنبَتَت سَبعَ سَنابِلَ فى كُلِّ سُنبُلَةٍ مِا۟ئَةُ حَبَّةٍ ۗ وَاللَّهُ يُضـٰعِفُ لِمَن يَشاءُ ۗ وَاللَّهُ وٰسِعٌ عَليمٌ

options: To guarantee a child will receive extra money tomorrow.
To encourage sincere spending in Allah’s cause and trust His reward.
To calculate a contest score for charity.
missions.anchor: FOCUS AYAHS: 2:261   |   CORE VALUES: Giving • Hope • Sincerity
missions.aim: Understand the Qur’anic example of a seed multiplying in connection with spending in Allah’s cause.
missions.meaning: Al-Baqarah 2:261 compares spending in Allah’s cause to a grain that produces seven ears, each containing a hundred grains; Allah multiplies as He wills.
missions.tafsir: The verse gives a vivid agricultural example of Allah’s reward for sincere spending in His path: one grain produces seven ears, each with a hundred grains. The purpose is to encourage generous obedience and trust in Allah, whose generosity is vast and whose knowledge encompasses people’s intentions. We should not turn the Qur’anic imagery into a guaranteed financial return, a game currency multiplier, or a claim that every small gift produces the same visible worldly outcome. Children can understand the example by planting a real seed, seeing how growth works, and reflecting that beneficial acts may reach farther than they first imagine. The purpose remains worship, not publicity or a contest. The verse refers to spending wealth, while classroom kindness is a supporting, age-appropriate application—not a replacement for the original subject.
missions.story: Imaan’s class planted seeds in small pots for the school courtyard. The teacher explained that one seed can grow into something much larger. Akhlaq connected this to a Qur’anic comparison they had read about giving. He suggested that the class also prepare a small, supervised collection of unused notebooks. They did not promise that every notebook would bring a visible reward; instead, they hoped the books would help others learn. Each pupil could participate freely, with no names posted or totals compared.
missions.question: Why does the Qur’an describe giving with the image of growing grain?
missions.feedback: Allah rewards as He wills. We never turn religious reward into a game guarantee.
missions.action: With permission, contribute one useful item or a little time to an approved helping effort.
missions.reflection: Why should we do good even when no one thanks us?
missions.vocabulary: Ḥabbah — grain/seed; Nafaqah — spending; Fī sabīlillāh — in Allah’s cause
missions.careNote: Do not gamify quantified spiritual reward or ask for money payments in the app.
missions.review: What Qur’anic principle guides your choice, and how is the modern story different from the original verse context?
missions.next: another thoughtful way to put mercy into practice.

missions.title: Help Without Hurting Feelings

ayahs.arabic: الَّذينَ يُنفِقونَ أَموٰلَهُم فى سَبيلِ اللَّهِ ثُمَّ لا يُتبِعونَ ما أَنفَقوا مَنًّا وَلا أَذًى ۙ لَهُم أَجرُهُم عِندَ رَبِّهِم وَلا خَوفٌ عَلَيهِم وَلا هُم يَحزَنونَ
قَولٌ مَعروفٌ وَمَغفِرَةٌ خَيرٌ مِن صَدَقَةٍ يَتبَعُها أَذًى ۗ وَاللَّهُ غَنِىٌّ حَليمٌ

options: Remind the whole class that they owe you.
Let them use the supplies without public reminders or demands.
Ask for a photo proving you helped.
missions.anchor: FOCUS AYAHS: 2:262, 2:263   |   CORE VALUES: Dignified charity • Kind speech • Humility
missions.aim: Give help respectfully, without boasting, reproach or humiliation.
missions.meaning: Al-Baqarah 2:262 praises those who spend without following gifts with reminders of their generosity or injury; 2:263 says kind words and forgiveness are better than charity followed by hurt.
missions.tafsir: These consecutive verses address the ethics of spending in Allah’s cause. Giving is not complete when a donor humiliates the recipient or repeatedly reminds them, “I did this for you.” Tafsir writers explain mann as boastful reminders and adha as harm through words or behavior. The following verse places kind speech and forgiveness above a gift followed by injury. Children need to understand that being unable to give an item is not permission to insult someone; a considerate answer is possible. Charity must also be truthful and safe; asking adults for help is appropriate. This lesson is not about making recipients grateful or obedient. It teaches the donor to protect the other person’s dignity. There is no app reward for uploading charity photos or revealing identities.
missions.story: Akhlaq shared a spare geometry set with a classmate, then mentioned the gift loudly each time they met. The classmate began avoiding him. Imaan asked how he might feel if someone told the whole class every time they helped him. Akhlaq realized that his words were turning a useful gift into embarrassment. He apologized quietly and stopped mentioning it. Their teacher later explained that helping someone and then hurting their feelings is not the kindness Allah asks us to practice.
missions.question: You shared supplies with someone. What should you do afterward?
missions.feedback: Respectful giving does not shame the recipient or demand praise.
missions.action: Offer one small helpful act without mentioning it to impress others.
missions.reflection: How can a gift become hurtful because of the words that follow?
missions.vocabulary: Mann — reproachful reminders; Adhā — hurt or injury; Qawl ma‘rūf — kind speech
missions.careNote: Do not require a donation or any recipient-identifying content.
missions.review: What Qur’anic principle guides your choice, and how is the modern story different from the original verse context?
missions.next: another thoughtful way to put mercy into practice.

missions.title: Strength Means Choosing Calm

ayahs.arabic: الَّذينَ يُنفِقونَ فِى السَّرّاءِ وَالضَّرّاءِ وَالكـٰظِمينَ الغَيظَ وَالعافينَ عَنِ النّاسِ ۗ وَاللَّهُ يُحِبُّ المُحسِنينَ

options: Shout and throw pieces at someone.
Hide your anger and never tell anyone.
Speak calmly and ask for appropriate help to repair the problem.
missions.anchor: FOCUS AYAHS: 3:134   |   CORE VALUES: Generosity • Controlling anger • Forgiveness
missions.aim: Practice a peaceful response when frustrated, while remembering the right to seek safety.
missions.meaning: Ali ‘Imran 3:134 praises those who spend in ease and difficulty, restrain anger and pardon people; Allah loves those who do good.
missions.tafsir: Within a description of the people of Taqwa, the verse praises generous spending in both ease and difficulty, the restraint of anger, and forgiving others. Controlling anger does not mean pretending to feel nothing. Children may breathe, step away, use respectful words, and speak to a trusted adult. Forgiveness also does not mean accepting bullying, abuse, unsafe behavior, or the loss of necessary boundaries. Tafsir connects these traits to ihsan: responding with goodness when it is difficult. Our story presents an everyday conflict in which a child can seek a fair solution without insulting another child. The original verse has a broader moral scope than any single classroom strategy. We cannot grade sincere forgiveness through a game, but we can help children recognize what patient, responsible responses look like.
missions.story: During a game, another child knocked over Akhlaq’s tower. He felt his face grow hot and wanted to shout. Imaan suggested that he first move the pieces out of the walkway, then tell the teacher what happened. The other child explained it had been an accident and offered to rebuild. Akhlaq still felt upset, but he decided to speak calmly and accept the help. Later, the teacher praised them for finding a fair solution rather than insulting each other.
missions.question: Your game project is accidentally damaged. What is a wise first step?
missions.feedback: You can feel upset, express it safely and seek help without hurting others.
missions.action: When frustrated today, pause and choose a respectful response before acting.
missions.reflection: What can I say when I feel angry but want to remain fair?
missions.vocabulary: Kāẓimīn al-ghayẓ — restraining anger; ‘Āfīn — those who pardon; Muḥsinīn — doers of good
missions.careNote: Never pressure a child to forgive a person who is harming them or to keep abuse secret.
missions.review: What Qur’anic principle guides your choice, and how is the modern story different from the original verse context?
missions.next: another thoughtful way to put mercy into practice.

missions.title: Forgiveness Without Losing Wisdom

ayahs.arabic: وَلا يَأتَلِ أُولُوا الفَضلِ مِنكُم وَالسَّعَةِ أَن يُؤتوا أُولِى القُربىٰ وَالمَسـٰكينَ وَالمُهـٰجِرينَ فى سَبيلِ اللَّهِ ۖ وَليَعفوا وَليَصفَحوا ۗ أَلا تُحِبّونَ أَن يَغفِرَ اللَّهُ لَكُم ۗ وَاللَّهُ غَفورٌ رَحيمٌ

options: Accept a fair repair plan and speak respectfully.
Tell everyone they are a terrible person.
Pretend nothing happened even if the problem remains.
missions.anchor: FOCUS AYAHS: 24:22   |   CORE VALUES: Forgiveness • Generosity • Healthy boundaries
missions.aim: Learn that forgiveness can restore kindness without requiring unsafe closeness.
missions.meaning: An-Nur 24:22 urges people of means not to stop helping relatives and others in need because of wrongdoing, and calls for forgiveness and pardon.
missions.tafsir: This verse has a specific historical context connected with Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (RA) and Mistah after the serious slander against ‘A’ishah (RA). Ibn Kathir and al-Tabari explain that Abu Bakr had resolved to stop financial assistance, and the revelation encouraged pardon and continuing good. The offense in the original account was grave; we must not reduce it to a casual playground dispute. For children, we can draw a narrower general lesson: when someone makes an ordinary mistake and sincerely tries to repair it, we can choose a kind response rather than nursing a grudge. Forgiveness does not erase accountability or require someone to remain near an unsafe person. Adults are responsible for handling significant harms and safeguarding children. Our fictional example is not the incident of revelation; it is a safe modern exercise in mercy and wisdom.
missions.story: Akhlaq and Mohsin were preparing a wall display when Mohsin accidentally smeared part of a painted poster. Mohsin apologized and offered to help repair it. Akhlaq was disappointed and considered refusing to work with him again. Imaan suggested a fair plan: Mohsin would help repaint the damaged area, and both would agree to handle wet paint carefully. Akhlaq accepted. He did not pretend the mistake never happened; he found a constructive way to move forward with respect.
missions.question: A friend accidentally damages your artwork, apologizes, and offers repair. What helps?
missions.feedback: Compassion can include apology, reasonable boundaries, and repair.
missions.action: If someone makes an ordinary mistake, offer a respectful path to make amends.
missions.reflection: How can forgiveness and responsibility work together?
missions.careNote: Provide adult-only historical background; never use the verse to demand reconciliation with an abuser.
missions.review: What Qur’anic principle guides your choice, and how is the modern story different from the original verse context?
missions.next: another thoughtful way to put mercy into practice.

missions.title: A Community That Makes Space for Others

ayahs.arabic: وَالَّذينَ تَبَوَّءُو الدّارَ وَالإيمـٰنَ مِن قَبلِهِم يُحِبّونَ مَن هاجَرَ إِلَيهِم وَلا يَجِدونَ فى صُدورِهِم حاجَةً مِمّا أوتوا وَيُؤثِرونَ عَلىٰ أَنفُسِهِم وَلَو كانَ بِهِم خَصاصَةٌ ۚ وَمَن يوقَ شُحَّ نَفسِهِ فَأُولـٰئِكَ هُمُ المُفلِحونَ

options: Tell them there is no room even when there is space.
Make room and explain the rules kindly.
Demand that another child give away something essential.
missions.anchor: FOCUS AYAHS: 59:9   |   CORE VALUES: Hospitality • Sharing • Brotherhood
missions.aim: Appreciate the generosity of the Ansar toward the Muhajirun, without pressuring children to deny their own needs.
missions.meaning: Al-Hashr 59:9 praises those settled in Madinah who welcomed emigrants, felt no resentment over what they received, and preferred others even despite personal need.
missions.tafsir: Surah Al-Hashr praises the Ansar of Madinah for their love of the emigrants, their freedom from resentment, and their remarkable readiness to give preference to others despite need. This is praise of real historical believers; their sacrifice should not be rewritten as a fictional classroom event. In an age-appropriate application, children can practise welcoming newcomers, sharing when they have something genuinely spare, and making room for another person in a group. The verse does not license teachers or peers to shame a child into surrendering necessary food, medicine, or possessions. Ikhthar, or selfless preference, is a voluntary virtue practiced with wisdom and responsibility. Gratitude and inclusion are often stronger when offered quietly, without expecting thanks.
missions.story: A new family arrived in Amanpur, and their children joined a community game day. Akhlaq noticed there were not enough chairs near the table, though several spare cushions were stored nearby. He and Imaan brought the cushions so everyone could join. Salamah greeted the new family and asked what activities their children enjoyed. Nobody demanded that anyone give up their lunch or personal belongings. The family felt welcomed because people had made room for them with thoughtfulness and respect.
missions.question: A new child joins your activity. What is a thoughtful response?
missions.feedback: Good hospitality includes welcoming others without unnecessary sacrifice or pressure.
missions.action: Make room for someone new in a safe shared activity.
missions.reflection: What does it feel like when people welcome us warmly?
missions.vocabulary: Anṣār — Helpers; Muhājirūn — Emigrants; Īthār — giving preference to others
missions.careNote: Never fictionalize the Companions’ direct speech. Child-centered scenes must be visibly modern fiction.
missions.review: What Qur’anic principle guides your choice, and how is the modern story different from the original verse context?
missions.next: another thoughtful way to put mercy into practice.

missions.title: Respond With What Is Better

ayahs.arabic: وَلا تَستَوِى الحَسَنَةُ وَلَا السَّيِّئَةُ ۚ ادفَع بِالَّتى هِىَ أَحسَنُ فَإِذَا الَّذى بَينَكَ وَبَينَهُ عَدٰوَةٌ كَأَنَّهُ وَلِىٌّ حَميمٌ

options: Speak respectfully and ask an adult for help if needed.
Reply with a stronger insult.
Agree to whatever they demand, even when unsafe.
missions.anchor: FOCUS AYAHS: 41:34   |   CORE VALUES: Gentleness • Self-control • Reconciliation
missions.aim: Choose a good response over a harsh reaction when a situation is safe.
missions.meaning: Fussilat 41:34 teaches that good and evil are not equal, and urges repelling wrongdoing with what is better; this can transform hostility into closeness.
missions.tafsir: The verse instructs the listener to repel bad behavior with something better. In Tafsir, this expresses patience, good speech, and wise treatment that can soften a hostile heart. It is not an absolute promise that an aggressive person will become friendly after one polite reply; nor is it permission to ignore danger. The original passage belongs to a wider discourse on calling to Allah and facing opposition. For children, an ordinary insult or misunderstanding may be met with calm correction, a refusal to exchange insults, or seeking help from an adult. The central lesson is that responding well often prevents a conflict from becoming worse. For serious bullying, threats, or harm, the “better” response may be moving away and reporting immediately, not engaging further.
missions.story: At the school gate, a classmate snapped at Akhlaq because the line was moving slowly. Akhlaq wanted to answer with a sharper insult. Imaan said, “We can ask for our turn without copying the rude words.” Akhlaq replied, “Let’s line up fairly. I can wait here.” The classmate was still annoyed, so the teacher organized the queue. Akhlaq did not win a magical friendship in an instant. He did, however, keep the disagreement from becoming a shouting match.
missions.question: Someone speaks rudely to you at school. Which is usually wisest when safe?
missions.feedback: The better response is calm, fair and safe—not surrendering boundaries.
missions.action: Replace one harsh reply with a respectful sentence today.
missions.reflection: When is leaving the situation the kindest and safest response?
missions.vocabulary: Aḥsan — better or best; Sayyi’ah — wrongdoing; Ḥamīm — close friend
missions.careNote: Do not promise friendship as the outcome or require victims to remain with aggressors.
missions.review: What Qur’anic principle guides your choice, and how is the modern story different from the original verse context?
missions.next: another thoughtful way to put mercy into practice.

missions.title: Cooperate in Good, Not in Harm

ayahs.arabic: يـٰأَيُّهَا الَّذينَ ءامَنوا لا تُحِلّوا شَعـٰئِرَ اللَّهِ وَلَا الشَّهرَ الحَرامَ وَلَا الهَدىَ وَلَا القَلـٰئِدَ وَلا ءامّينَ البَيتَ الحَرامَ يَبتَغونَ فَضلًا مِن رَبِّهِم وَرِضوٰنًا ۚ وَإِذا حَلَلتُم فَاصطادوا ۚ وَلا يَجرِمَنَّكُم شَنَـٔانُ قَومٍ أَن صَدّوكُم عَنِ المَسجِدِ الحَرامِ أَن تَعتَدوا ۘ وَتَعاوَنوا عَلَى البِرِّ وَالتَّقوىٰ ۖ وَلا تَعاوَنوا عَلَى الإِثمِ وَالعُدوٰنِ ۚ وَاتَّقُوا اللَّهَ ۖ إِنَّ اللَّهَ شَديدُ العِقابِ

options: Join in because most teammates agree.
Say no politely and suggest asking permission or finding another way.
Keep quiet but take the materials later.
missions.anchor: FOCUS AYAHS: 5:2   |   CORE VALUES: Cooperation • Choosing good companions • Safety
missions.aim: Identify helpful cooperation and refuse group pressure toward harmful actions.
missions.meaning: A clause within Al-Ma’idah 5:2 commands cooperation in righteousness and piety, and forbids cooperation in sin and aggression. The complete ayah also discusses sacred rites and respectful conduct in the pilgrimage context.
missions.memorization:
وَتَعاوَنوا عَلَى البِرِّ وَالتَّقوىٰ ۖ وَلا تَعاوَنوا عَلَى الإِثمِ وَالعُدوٰنِ

This is only a short phrase from 5:2 for learning; the complete ayah above remains primary.
missions.tafsir: The central phrase of Al-Ma’idah 5:2 calls people to cooperate in birr and taqwa rather than in wrongdoing and aggression. The whole verse also gives instructions about sacred symbols and conduct near the Sacred Mosque, as well as not allowing hatred to cause transgression. The child-facing teaching must keep this context available. In everyday life, cooperation can mean working together for clean spaces, helping someone study, or reporting unsafe behavior. A group is not automatically right because many people agree. Children may refuse an invitation to exclude, mock, or cheat. Working together is a virtue when the goal and means are good; refusing harmful group pressure is also a kind of responsible teamwork. The game must not equate genuine religious law with class rules, but it can draw a careful ethical application.
missions.story: Four students were building a garden bench for a school project. Two wanted to take materials from another group without permission. Akhlaq felt pressured because everyone wanted to finish first. Imaan suggested asking the teacher for the proper supplies and sharing tools on a timetable. The other students agreed to try. Their bench took a little longer, but they completed it fairly. Akhlaq realized that teamwork does not mean joining every plan; good cooperation has good boundaries.
missions.question: Your team asks you to use another group’s materials without permission. What should you do?
missions.feedback: Good teamwork helps others without taking what is not ours.
missions.action: Join one safe group activity that benefits others and respects everyone’s rights.
missions.reflection: How can I be a good teammate without agreeing to something wrong?
missions.vocabulary: Ta‘āwun — cooperation; Birr — righteousness; Taqwā — mindfulness of Allah
missions.careNote: Show the entire 5:2 ayah in context; the memo text is an excerpt and must be labeled.
missions.review: What Qur’anic principle guides your choice, and how is the modern story different from the original verse context?
missions.next: another thoughtful way to put mercy into practice.

missions.title: Whom Should We Help?

ayahs.arabic: يَسـَٔلونَكَ ماذا يُنفِقونَ ۖ قُل ما أَنفَقتُم مِن خَيرٍ فَلِلوٰلِدَينِ وَالأَقرَبينَ وَاليَتـٰمىٰ وَالمَسـٰكينِ وَابنِ السَّبيلِ ۗ وَما تَفعَلوا مِن خَيرٍ فَإِنَّ اللَّهَ بِهِ عَليمٌ

options: Decide who deserves help by appearance.
Post photos of recipients to prove the project worked.
Ask trusted adults what is genuinely useful and contribute safely.
missions.anchor: FOCUS AYAHS: 2:215   |   CORE VALUES: Generosity • Family needs • Social responsibility
missions.aim: Understand the groups named in the Qur’an as appropriate recipients of charitable spending.
missions.meaning: Al-Baqarah 2:215 responds to a question about spending, naming parents, near relatives, orphans, needy people and travelers; Allah knows every good done.
missions.tafsir: Al-Baqarah 2:215 answers a question about what to spend by directing attention toward parents, relatives, orphans, people in need, and travelers. It teaches that charitable spending should be thoughtful and benefit those with rights and genuine needs. The verse concerns wealth and responsibility; young children should not feel obliged to donate cash, manage family budgets or decide who “deserves” help. Adults can explain the categories with dignity and allow safe ways for children to contribute, such as preparing a card for an ill relative, helping to sort family supplies, or giving a little supervised time. The verse also reminds us that Allah knows the good we do, so public proof is unnecessary. The mission concludes the volume by moving from feeling compassion toward choosing appropriate, responsible actions.
missions.story: Amanpur School invited families to suggest a community care project. Akhlaq proposed a large, colorful collection box. Imaan wondered who would decide what was actually needed. Their teacher invited a local volunteer to explain how families could offer help privately and safely. The class chose to prepare useful stationery packs with parental permission. They made a simple sign saying, “Everyone is welcome to learn.” They did not list recipients or measure which child gave the most. Their work was thoughtful because they first listened, then helped.
missions.question: How should children take part in helping people in need?
missions.feedback: Thoughtful generosity begins with dignity, consultation and proper care.
missions.action: Ask a trusted adult about one useful, safe way your family or class can support others.
missions.reflection: What is the difference between helping someone and showing off that we helped?
missions.vocabulary: Infāq — charitable spending; Khayr — good; Qarābah — relatives
missions.careNote: No public donation totals, recipient profiles, or financial pressure on children.
missions.review: What Qur’anic principle guides your choice, and how is the modern story different from the original verse context?
